t: from the consecrated property for the upkeep of the Temple (bedek habayit). Consecrations of things not meant for the altar and which are used (or their proceeds are used) for repair of the Temple and its other needs.
me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property). Its law will be explained below, halakhah 3.

the two loaves after the sprinkling of the blood of the two lambs. On Shavuot two lambs are offered as peace offerings. Offering the lambs permits eating the two loaves brought with them (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 8:11).

even if a non-priest ate of these and the like etc.. Although a non-priest who eats these things transgresses a prohibition (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:8), since they are permitted to priests, they are not subject to the law of me'ilah.
even if they were disqualified and forbidden to eat. And now they are forbidden to eat for everyone, and one who eats of them transgresses a prohibition (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:3-4).
at its principal. The principal value of what he damaged, without the addition.

from tradition they learned that this is a warning for one who eats the flesh of a burnt offering. The prohibition of eating "your vows" refers to eating the flesh of a burnt offering (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:1).
for it is the Lord's alone. And no one else may benefit from it.
what he benefited and an added fifth. He adds a quarter to the principal, and after the addition the addition is a fifth of everything he brings (below, halakhah 5).
a ram worth two sela'im. A two-year-old ram worth two sela coins.
they hold back the atonement. As long as he has not brought them, the sin remains upon him.
the ram and the guilt offering. Bringing the ram and paying the principal.
he brought his me'ilah before he brought his guilt offering. He brought the offering before paying the principal.

and the fifth is like the original consecration, and if he benefited from it he adds a fifth on the fifth. Although the fifth was not directly consecrated to the Temple treasury, one who benefits from it pays for the me'ilah as he pays for any me'ilah: he brings the price of the fifth as principal and adds a fifth to it.
and we have already explained several times. Hilchot Terumot 10:26, Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:1, Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 4:5.

that the fifth is one fourth of the principal, so that it and its fifth make five. When he adds a quarter of the principal to the principal, the addition is a fifth of everything he pays. For example, if the principal is a hundred, he must add twenty-five, which is a quarter of a hundred, and a fifth of one hundred twenty-five, the total he pays.
there are things for which one is not liable etc.. For example, a sacrificial animal that died (below 3:1).
all altar offerings. See below, halakhah 12, regarding the prohibition of shearing and working with Temple-upkeep consecrated animals.
and the same applies to other sacred things. Except for a firstborn.
one who shears a bull or works with a flock animal is flogged by Torah law. The shearing and working were prohibited in all kinds of animals (not only working a bull and shearing a sheep).
and plucking is not like shearing. Plucking wool by hand is not prohibited by the Torah like plucking with a tool (and sometimes it is permitted even initially - see below, halakhot 10-11).

the width of a double sit etc.. That he shear wool from which a thread can be spun four handbreadths long, which is twice the distance between the thumb and forefinger (the width of a sit). This is the measure for liability for one who performs the labor of shearing on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 9:7).
that developed a blemish and was redeemed, as we explained. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10.
and it remains in its prohibition. The prohibition of shearing and working remains on it as it was before the redemption.
if it was slaughtered after its redemption, it is permitted to be eaten. Like ordinary unconsecrated meat.
when their consecration preceded their blemish. They consecrated them unblemished, and afterward a blemish developed in them.

a transient blemish preceded their consecration. They consecrated them with a transient blemish (so that the offering is disqualified from being offered until the blemish passes), and afterward a permanent blemish developed. In these cases full sanctity took effect on their bodies before they became blemished and completely disqualified from offering.

one who consecrates an animal with a permanent blemish to the altar, it is not prohibited etc.. When it was entirely disqualified from offering from the start of the consecration, sanctity did not take effect on its body but only on its value (ibid. halakhah 11).
only by rabbinic law. Like all Temple-upkeep consecrations, which are prohibited from shearing and working by rabbinic law (below, halakhah 12).

except for a firstborn and a tithe animal, whose sanctity takes effect on their bodies etc.. The sanctity of the firstborn and the tithe is not by verbal consecration, but their sanctity comes from the womb (firstborn) or from their leaving the pen (the tenth animal that leaves the pen is sacred with the sanctity of tithe, Hilchot Bechorot 7:1), and therefore their sanctity takes effect even on blemished animals.

and it is forbidden to breed a firstborn or disqualified consecrated animals. Breeding is considered the work forbidden with sacred animals (Minchat Chinuch; and see Hilchot Kilayim 9:11 regarding the prohibition of mixed breeding with disqualified consecrated animals).
it is permitted to pluck the hair initially. By hand. And it must be left tangled in the wool as with one who plucks to slaughter, mentioned below, halakhah 11 (Minchat Chinuch).
to show the blemish to an expert. The permission of a firstborn to be slaughtered with its blemish is given by an expert authorized for this by the nasi of the Sanhedrin (Hilchot Bechorot 3:1).
and that hair which he plucked. Permissibly, to show the expert.

a decree lest he keep them, since they do not come for atonement. Since the firstborn and the tithe do not atone, there is concern that he may keep them to benefit from their wool and not hurry to offer them.

what falls from a sin offering and a guilt offering is permitted for use after they are slaughtered because of their blemish. If a blemish develops in them and they are slaughtered (after redemption), it will be permitted to use the hair even if it fell before the animal developed a blemish.

and if it was plucked from a burnt offering, it is in doubt. Although a burnt offering atones for neglect of a positive commandment, its essence is not atonement for sin but a freewill gift of the heart (Bavli Bechorot 26b).
for he did not pluck it by hand. But hair plucked in violation is forbidden in all sacred animals, unblemished and blemished (Ri Kapach).
except for the firstborn. And the tithe, both of which do not come for atonement, and they decreed a prohibition on their hair even when plucked after they became blemished (Hilchot Bechorot 3:11).

provided that he does not move it from its place. He should not take the plucked hair but leave it tangled in the wool (similarly they permitted one who slaughters on a festival to pluck the wool by hand - Hilchot Yom Tov 3:3).
rebellion lashes. Lashes by rabbinic law.
he consecrated one limb of an animal. If he consecrated a limb on which the animal's life does not depend.

whether for Temple upkeep or for the altar. For when he consecrates an animal fit for the altar, even if he consecrates it for Temple upkeep, its law is that it is offered on the altar (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 5:5).

lesser sacrifices: there is no me'ilah in them until the blood is sprinkled. Until the blood is sprinkled they are not yet considered the Lord's sacred property, and therefore there is no me'ilah in them (see above 1:1-2).

once the blood is sprinkled, there is me'ilah in their sacrificial portions. By the sprinkling of the blood the sacrificial portions were made fit for burning on the altar, and therefore there is me'ilah in them.

until they go out to the place of the ashes. Even after the sacrificial portions are burned, there is me'ilah in their ashes until their commandment is completed by taking them out to the ash dump outside the city, where the altar ashes were brought.
and there is no me'ilah with something edible, as we explained. Above 1:2.

even if he brought up their sacrificial portions to the altar before sprinkling etc.. Although as soon as they were placed up they became "the altar's bread" and may not be taken down (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:12), until the sprinkling they are not the Lord's sacred property and there is no me'ilah in them.
outside. Outside the Temple court.
there is no me'ilah in them until the blood is sprinkled. Just as there is no me'ilah in the sacrificial portions that are inside until the sprinkling.

once the blood is sprinkled, even though they are still outside etc.. The sprinkling of the blood makes fit for burning also the sacrificial portions that are outside (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:33), and therefore there is me'ilah in them.

for the sprinkling is effective for what went out, both to be lenient and to be stringent. The sprinkling of the blood works both to make the sacrificial portions of lesser sacrifices that are outside liable to me'ilah, and to exempt the flesh of most sacred sacrifices that are eaten from me'ilah (for after the blood is sprinkled there is no me'ilah in it, as above 2:1).

from when they are consecrated until the blood is sprinkled etc.. From the moment the animal is consecrated until the blood is sprinkled there is me'ilah in all of it, and after the sprinkling there is me'ilah only in its parts that are not eaten.
and there is no me'ilah with something edible, as we explained. Above 1:2.
the priests' meal offering, the chavitin, and the meal offering of libations. These meal offerings are burned and have no edible portion.
bulls that are burned and goats that are burned. Sin offerings that are burned.
that they be burned and their burning be completed at the place of the ashes. Their burning is done at the ash dump outside the city (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:2).
and the flesh melts away. It burns entirely and becomes hollow like a sponge (Commentary on the Mishnah, Me'ilah 2:3).

even though it is like Temple-upkeep consecrations. For there is me'ilah in them until they are redeemed and made ordinary (below 5:1), and therefore one might have thought there is me'ilah also in the ashes of the red heifer (Ri Kapach, Chiddushei R. Chaim HaLevi).
it is said of it, "it is a sin offering". Therefore by Torah law the law of its ashes is like that of sacrifices, and there is no me'ilah in them after burning.

and it is a stipulation of the court that no one commit me'ilah with the ashes of the heifer. The court enacted that even by rabbinic law there be no me'ilah in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 7:7, based on Bavli Menachot 51b-52a).
an animal sin offering, a guilt offering, and the peace offerings of the community. Most sacred offerings that are eaten.
and there is no me'ilah in the flesh. Since it became permitted to the priests for eating by the sprinkling of the blood.
its blood was sprinkled, there is no me'ilah in it. For all its flesh is eaten.
with its crop and its feathers. The crop and the skin on it.
meal offerings: there is me'ilah in them from when they are consecrated. Meal offerings are considered most sacred, and therefore there is me'ilah in them from the moment they are consecrated.
even though they have not yet been sanctified in a service vessel. Although they are not yet sacred with the sanctity of the body, so as to be disqualified by being left overnight and the like.

once the kometz is offered, the remainder is permitted for eating. And there is no me'ilah in them. But in the kometz that is burned there is me'ilah until it goes out to the ash dump, like the other offerings burned on the altar.

the remainder was disqualified. The remainder itself was disqualified, for example if the flour became wormy (but if it became impure or went out, there is no me'ilah in them, as below 3:9, Birkat HaZevach, Me'ilah 7:2).
since this burning does not permit the remainder for eating. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:20.
even though it has not yet been baked. And it has not been sanctified with the sanctity of the body.

until he burns the bazikhin etc.. The two bowls of frankincense that are set beside the bread on the table and burned on the altar on Shabbat. Their burning permits eating the bread, and therefore after the burning of the bowls there is no me'ilah in it.

and likewise the two loaves etc.. Brought on Shavuot with the two lambs. Sprinkling the blood of the lambs permits the bread for eating, and therefore after the sprinkling of the blood there is no me'ilah in them.
the libations. The wine poured on the altar with the burnt offerings and peace offerings.

went down to the pits. The wine went down from the altar through two openings called the shittin, and drained into the cavity beneath the altar called the shit (Commentary on the Mishnah, Middot 3:3). The wine's reaching the shittin completes its commandment, and after that there is no me'ilah in it.
the water that is poured on Sukkot. On Sukkot, together with the pouring of the wine of the morning tamid, water was also poured (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:6).

as long as they are in the golden jug... they put it in the flask. Each day they filled the water from the Shiloach with a golden flask, and from this flask they poured the water on the altar (ibid. halakhah 7). On Friday they would fill the water for the Shabbat pouring in a golden jug that was not sanctified (so that the water in it would not be disqualified by being left overnight, ibid. halakhah 9), and therefore as long as the water is in the jug there is no me'ilah in it, but by rabbinic law it is forbidden to benefit from it.

the log of oil of the leper. The leper brings a log of oil with his guilt offering. Some of the oil was sprinkled toward the Holy of Holies and placed on the ear lobe and thumbs of the leper, and the rest of the oil was eaten by the priests (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).
they neither benefit nor commit me'ilah. There is no Torah prohibition of me'ilah, but by rabbinic law it is forbidden to benefit from the oil.
until they have given some of it as the gifts. On the ear lobe and thumbs of the leper.
whether before atonement or after atonement. Before and after it was sprinkled on the altar.

until it goes out to the Kidron stream etc.. The blood in the Temple court drained into a channel and went out to the Kidron stream, where it was sold as fertilizer to gardeners, and therefore its law is like Temple-upkeep consecrations, in which there is me'ilah.
but one who lets blood from a sacrificial animal. Before it is slaughtered.
the bones, sinews, horns, and hooves. Parts of the animal that are not fit for eating or burning (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 14:7).

that separated from most sacred offerings before the sprinkling of the blood, there is me'ilah in them. Since they were not attached to the flesh, the sprinkling of the blood does not permit them and the prohibition of me'ilah remains on them (Ri Kapach, Kiryat Sefer; and Kesef Mishneh explained that there is me'ilah in them only until the time of the sprinkling).
if they separated after the sprinkling of the blood, there is no me'ilah in them. Since they were attached to the flesh at the time of the sprinkling, they were permitted along with it.

the bones of the burnt offering that separated before sprinkling etc.. Since they separated from the flesh, they are not burned on the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:2), and therefore after the sprinkling it is permitted to benefit from them (and see Chelkat Yoav, Me'ilah 1:7, who discusses the difference between a burnt offering and other most sacred offerings).

and if they separated after the sprinkling, there is me'ilah in them forever. Since at the time of the sprinkling they were attached to the flesh that is to be burned, the law of the flesh applies to them and there is me'ilah in them.

the bones of the burnt offering that burst off the altar etc.. Bones that burst off the altar have the law of dry flesh that burst off the altar, which must be put back and burned until midnight (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:3). Therefore until midnight there is me'ilah in them, and after midnight there is no me'ilah in them.
a coal. A glowing piece from the fire arrangement.

they neither benefit nor commit me'ilah. In every case where it bursts off it is not to be returned to the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:2), and therefore there is no me'ilah in it. However, it is forbidden to benefit from it, since it has substance (Bavli Me'ilah 9b).
a coal of Temple-upkeep consecrations, there is me'ilah in it. Since it has substance, its law is like all Temple-upkeep consecrations and there is me'ilah in it.
and the flame, they neither benefit nor commit me'ilah. Since it has no substance there is no me'ilah in it.

whether before the removal of the ashes or after the removal. Every day they took ashes from the altar and placed them on the east side of the ramp (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:10-12). Even after the removal of the ashes, there is the law of me'ilah for ashes remaining on the altar.
there is me'ilah in it. Until it is taken outside the city to the ash dump. However, even after it is taken out, it is forbidden to benefit from it (ibid. halakhah 15 and Ri Kapach there).
the ashes of the inner altar and the ashes of the menorah. The ashes of the incense and the ashes of the menorah.
they do not benefit. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:13.

whether a permanent blemish preceded its consecration. And there is no sanctity in its body, but nevertheless there is sanctity in its value and its law is similar to Temple-upkeep consecrations, in which there is me'ilah (Ri Kapach, and see below 3:13).
when its consecration preceded a permanent blemish. And when he consecrated it, full sanctity took effect on it.
even if it was lacking in time. An animal within the first seven days of its birth, which is forbidden to offer (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8).
there is me'ilah in them from when they are consecrated until they are redeemed. Until they are sold and their value takes on the sanctity in their place (ibid. 1:10).
but turtledoves whose time has not come and young pigeons whose time has passed. Young turtledoves and grown pigeons (turtledoves are fit only when grown and pigeons only when young - ibid. 3:2).
since they are not fit for redemption. See ibid. 6:4.
they are like the sin offerings that are to die. Sin offerings whose law is to die and in which there is no me'ilah (below 3:4).
therefore there is no me'ilah in them. For they are not now fit for the altar and there is no possibility of deriving monetary value from them (Keren Orah, Me'ilah 12:1).
altar offerings that died. Their law is that they are buried (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:11), and since that is so, they are not the Lord's sacred property and there is no Torah me'ilah in them.
if they were disqualified through things by which offerings are disqualified. In all the ways in which offerings are disqualified.
which we already explained. In Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin.
where they never had a time of permission for the priests to eat. Before they were disqualified.
as we explained. Above 1:2.
in all these there is me'ilah in all of them forever. By rabbinic law.
but if the blood reached the altar as required etc.. In all of these the flesh became permitted for eating before it was disqualified.

or if part of the flesh went out before the sprinkling of the blood etc.. In this case part of the flesh was disqualified before the sprinkling but the other part was permitted by the sprinkling, and therefore there is no me'ilah even in the rest of the flesh that went out and was disqualified from eating.
and they received the rest of the life-blood. The blood remaining in the neck through which the life departs, the blood fit for the altar.

for the disqualified do not make the rest of the life-blood into remainder. The sprinkling by disqualified people does not disqualify the life-blood that remains in the animal's neck (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:28). Therefore if qualified people received and sprinkled the remaining blood, the offering is valid, its flesh is permitted for eating, and there is no me'ilah in it.

except for the impure etc.. When there are no pure people, an impure person may offer community offerings (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:9). Therefore when an impure person received and sprinkled the blood, the offering is disqualified even if life-blood remained in the neck (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin ibid.).
and there is me'ilah in all of them. In the flesh and in the sacrificial portions.
and the sprinkling of the remainder does not take effect. Sprinkling the blood of the disqualified remainder does not permit the flesh for eating or remove it from me'ilah.
we already explained. Above 2:1.
provided that it is a sprinkling that is effective. A valid sprinkling by which the sacrificial portions become fit for the altar.
that became piggul. Disqualified through an improper intention.
the blood went out. From the Temple court and became disqualified.

sin offerings that are to die, such as the offspring of a sin offering, its substitute, and the like. Sin offerings whose law is to die (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1), which are not fit for the altar and may not be redeemed (see above 2:16).

a sin offering that grazes until it develops a blemish. A sin offering that cannot be used for atonement and is not among the sin offerings that die must wait until a blemish develops in it and then be redeemed (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin chapter 4).
there is me'ilah in it until it is redeemed. Like other blemished animals before redemption (above 2:16).
one who sets aside his sin offering and it was lost, and he set aside another etc.. He may slaughter and gain atonement with either of them (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:3).
not in the flesh of the one whose blood was sprinkled. For it was permitted for eating.

since if he wished he could sprinkle from this one, and if he wished he could sprinkle from that one. Since he can sprinkle from the blood of either, the sprinkling of one works to remove both from me'ilah.
for it did not have a time fit for permission of its flesh. When the first was slaughtered the second was disqualified, and there was no time when the blood of the second could have been sprinkled.

any bird sin offering or bird burnt offering that was disqualified etc.. A bird sin offering is done below, on the lower part of the altar, and the head is not separated from the body when pinching its neck. A bird burnt offering is done above, on the upper part of the altar, and the head is separated from the body when pinching its neck. If he changed and did the sin offering as a burnt offering or the burnt offering as a sin offering, the offering is disqualified and there is me'ilah in it (by rabbinic law) like most sacred offerings that were disqualified (above, halakhah 1).

even though it did not count for the owners as an obligatory offering etc.. Although the offering was disqualified and one cannot fulfill the obligation with it as a sin offering, for the law of me'ilah, doing the burnt offering in the place and manner in which the sin offering is done makes it like a bird sin offering, all of whose flesh is eaten and in which there is no me'ilah after the sprinkling of the blood.
a meal offering that became piggul. Disqualified when they intended to eat or burn it after its proper time.
that was done with an intention concerning place. Disqualified when they intended to eat or burn it outside the Temple court.

there is me'ilah in them, for they never had a time of permission. Had they been done properly they would have left the status of me'ilah, since they would have become permitted for eating. But when disqualified they were not permitted for eating, and the prohibition of me'ilah remained on them.
and he again burned it. Since it was disqualified, this burning does not permit the remainder for eating.

there is no me'ilah in the remainder where the tzitz atones etc.. A meal offering whose kometz became impure and was burned is accepted by the tzitz (one fulfills the obligation with it), and there is no me'ilah in its remainder, like the remainder of all meal offerings after the burning of the kometz.
for the tzitz atones for the impure etc.. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:19.

the remainder went out or became impure. Some wrote that this speaks of when part of the remainder went out or became impure, but when all the remainder went out or became impure there is me'ilah in it, as in flesh that went out or became impure entirely before sprinkling (above, halakhah 1 - Ri Kapach, Kesef Mishneh and others). And some wrote that this speaks even when all the remainder went out or became impure, and distinguished between the flesh of offerings and the remainder of meal offerings (see Or Sameach, Even HaEzel and others).
even though they are forbidden for eating. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:20.
there is no me'ilah in them, for the kometz was offered as required. And it is for another reason that the remainder may not be eaten (see above 2:7).
one who benefits from all most sacred offerings. The flesh and the sacrificial portions.

who benefited from the entire burnt offering etc.. Even after the sprinkling of the blood, since it is burned entirely (and the same applies when he benefited from the sacrificial portions of most sacred offerings after the sprinkling).
what he benefited shall go to a freewill offering. For a community freewill burnt offering.

if he committed me'ilah with community offerings, what he benefited shall go to the chamber. To the Temple upkeep (Kesef Mishneh; and the Ri Kapach wrote that the money is given to the terumat halishkah from which community offerings were bought).

if he benefited before the sprinkling from the flesh of most sacred offerings that became impure... he is exempt. Since the flesh became impure and must be burned, there is no me'ilah in it (and the commentators wondered why there is not me'ilah in it by rabbinic law, as above, halakhah 1).

from the sacrificial portions of lesser sacrifices, even though he brought them up to the top of the altar, he is exempt. Even though it has already reached the altar, since the blood has not yet been sprinkled there is no me'ilah in them (see also above 2:1).

and a person may pledge and say, the milk of this animal etc.. Since the offspring of consecrated animals cannot nurse from their mothers, people would consecrate the milk of their animals for the offspring of sacred animals (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Me'ilah 3:7).
and likewise the offspring of the tithe animal. The animal tithe.
it may not nurse from its mother. For it is forbidden to benefit from its milk.

the value of this animal for libations and the value of this young pigeon for peace offerings. When he consecrated them for something that cannot be offered from them, they must be sold and his obligation brought from their proceeds (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:5), and therefore their law is like Temple-upkeep consecrations and there is me'ilah also in their milk and eggs.
as will be explained. Below 5:13.

one who sets aside money for his sin offering etc.. When he sets aside money to buy an offering with it, their law regarding me'ilah is like that of the offering itself: if he set it aside for a most sacred offering there is me'ilah in it from the moment of setting aside, and if he set it aside for a lesser sacrifice there is no me'ilah in it, just as there is no me'ilah in lesser sacrifices (except in the sacrificial portions after the sprinkling of the blood, above 2:1).
he consecrated one limb for its value to the altar. He consecrated only the value of a hand or foot of the animal.

it is in doubt whether the sanctity spread through all of it or did not spread. When one consecrates an entire animal for its value, it becomes sacred with the sanctity of the body and must be offered. When he consecrates one limb, there is doubt whether the sanctity spreads through all of it or not (see also Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 5:14).

therefore it should be offered and not redeemed, and if it was redeemed there is no me'ilah in its redemption. Because of the doubt whether the sanctity spread through all of it, it must be offered and cannot be redeemed. And if he redeemed it anyway, there is no me'ilah in the money, for if it is indeed sacred it cannot be redeemed and the redemption money is ordinary (Ri Kapach).

one who sets aside money for his naziriteship. To bring offerings with it: a sin offering, a burnt offering and peace offerings. This speaks of unspecified money, that is, he set aside money to bring his offerings from it and said nothing (Hilchot Nezirut 9:4).
and if he benefited he did not commit me'ilah, because all of it is fit to come as peace offerings. Since he could bring peace offerings with all the money, there is no me'ilah in it.

if he died, it shall fall to freewill offerings. It is a halakhah of Moses from Sinai that unspecified nazirite money of a nazirite who died falls to freewill offerings (Bavli Nazir 25a, and see also Hilchot Nezirut 9:3).
they were specified. For example, he said the money is for his burnt offering, his sin offering and his peace offering (ibid. halakhah 4).

the value of the sin offering goes to the Dead Sea, and they neither benefit nor commit me'ilah. The value of a sin offering whose owners died goes to the Dead Sea (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:1), and just as there is no me'ilah in sin offerings that die (above 3:4), so there is none in this money.

the value of the burnt offering shall be brought as a burnt offering and there is me'ilah in it. They bring a burnt offering after the owners' death (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:9). Likewise the value of peace offerings is used to bring peace offerings, which are eaten for one day and do not require bread (Hilchot Nezirut 9:3).
these for my sin offering and the rest for my naziriteship. He set aside part of the money for a sin offering and the rest for the burnt offering and peace offerings.

if he benefited from all the rest he committed me'ilah, if he benefited from part of it he did not commit me'ilah. When he benefited from all of it, he committed me'ilah in the burnt offering portion mixed in the money. But if he benefited from part of the money, he did not commit me'ilah, since that part is fit to be peace offerings.

and the rest for my naziriteship and he benefited from all of them, he committed me'ilah; if he benefited from part of them he did not commit me'ilah. For the value of the sin offering (in which there is me'ilah) and peace offerings (in which there is none) is mixed in this money.

there is me'ilah in all of them and there is me'ilah in part of them. Because of the value of the sin offering and the burnt offering mixed in them (and see commentators who discussed why there is me'ilah in part of them when some of the money is for peace offerings, and see also below 7:7).
and how should he proceed. How should he use this money to bring his offerings.

and he transfers the sanctity of the sin offering's value to any animal he chooses etc.. He transfers the sanctity of the sin offering's value to one of the animals and it becomes a sin offering, and likewise he does for the burnt offering and peace offerings with the other two animals.
from those obligated to bring birds. One obligated to bring two birds, for a sin offering and a burnt offering.
there is me'ilah in all of them and there is me'ilah in part of them. Both in the value of the sin offering and in the value of the burnt offering there is me'ilah.

and if he died, it shall fall to freewill offerings. Although it includes the value of a sin offering whose owners died, which normally goes to the Dead Sea and has no me'ilah, for bird offerings (like a nazirite) it is a halakhah of Moses from Sinai that the value of the bird offerings falls to freewill offerings, and therefore there is me'ilah in it (Bavli Nazir 26a).
as we explained regarding naziriteship. Regarding the law of unspecified nazirite money (Hilchot Nezirut 9:3, above, halakhah 3).

he did not atone. Although he was obligated to bring a sin offering also for eating blood, he does not fulfill with this sin offering the obligation of eating blood (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:6).
therefore he did not commit me'ilah. Since he did not benefit through offering the sin offering.

if inadvertent, he atoned, therefore he committed me'ilah; if deliberate, he did not atone, therefore he did not commit me'ilah. When he uses the offering money inadvertently, it leaves sanctity (see below 6:3), and when he buys with it an animal for another offering he gains atonement through it, and therefore he committed me'ilah. But if he uses it deliberately the money remains in its sanctity, and when he changes it from a fat sin offering to a blood sin offering he did not atone and did not commit me'ilah.
two sela'im for a guilt offering. All guilt offerings, except the leper's guilt offering and the nazirite's guilt offering, must be worth at least two sela'im (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:22).
ten dinars, which are two sela'im and their fifth. Since a sela is four dinars, the principal and the fifth of two sela'im come to ten dinars.

and he shall bring a guilt offering with them. He brings with the money the guilt offering for which he was originally obligated, and for which the two sela'im were consecrated (like one who commits me'ilah with the money of offerings and brings with the principal and fifth the offering in which he committed me'ilah, below, halakhah 7).

he shall bring one worth ten as a guilt offering in place of the me'ilah, with the fifth. The ram worth ten is brought in place of the guilt offering he was originally obligated to bring, with whose money he committed me'ilah, so the ten dinars are payment for the eight dinars with which he committed me'ilah, plus a fifth.
and he shall bring one worth two sela'im as a guilt offering for his me'ilah. The guilt offering of me'ilah for having committed me'ilah.
he bought one for a guilt offering and one for ordinary use. And he committed me'ilah with only one of the two sela'im.
if the guilt offering was worth two sela'im. For example, if the price of the ram rose and it is now worth two sela'im.
he brings it for his first guilt offering. The guilt offering for which he was originally obligated.

and likewise if this ordinary one was worth two, he brings it as his guilt offering for me'ilah. The guilt offering of me'ilah that he owes he can bring from the ram he bought for ordinary use if it is worth two sela'im.

and he pays five dinars, which fall to freewill offerings. Since he bought a ram for a guilt offering with one sela, the second sela is considered surplus of a guilt offering and its law is to fall to freewill offerings (below, halakhah 7). Therefore if he committed me'ilah with it, he brings five dinars, the principal and fifth for the sela with which he committed me'ilah, and they fall to freewill offerings.

one who benefited from the value of a sin offering before his sin offering was offered. He committed me'ilah with money he set aside to bring a sin offering, and has not yet brought another sin offering.

for the me'ilah of altar offerings goes to altar offerings. With the me'ilah money he must buy the offering in which he committed me'ilah (and see above 3:10 regarding me'ilah in community offerings).
he learned that he committed me'ilah. And as soon as he learned of the me'ilah he became obligated in the principal and fifth that are designated for the offering of his sin offering.
and afterward his sin offering was offered. From other money.

or he set it aside and did not include it in the value of his sin offering. He bought the sin offering with other money and not with the me'ilah money and its fifth (even if he has not yet offered the sin offering).

he takes the me'ilah and its fifth to the Dead Sea. Like the law of two sin offerings designated for offering, where one is separated and the other must die (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:3), and therefore the law of the money is to go to the Dead Sea (Ri Kapach).

he learned that he committed me'ilah after his sin offering was offered. So reads the manuscript version. In the printed editions the reading is: "he learned that he committed me'ilah after his sin offering was offered."

for one does not initially set aside money to be destroyed. Only in the case where he was obligated to set aside money for a sin offering and then their law was fixed as going to the Dead Sea do they destroy the money. But if at the time of the obligation their law was already to be destroyed, one does not set it aside for that but for freewill offerings (community freewill burnt offerings).
because it is like surplus of a guilt offering. And its law is to fall to freewill offerings (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 5:9).
he did nothing. The sale does not take effect.
and the law of the Torah is that the money return to being ordinary as it was. Since the sale was annulled, the money should return to the buyer and be ordinary.
and they penalized him. The buyer, so that he not again buy the offerings of others (Rashi, Pesachim 89b).
there is me'ilah with vows. When he benefited from something forbidden by a vow.
this loaf is upon me as an offering or as consecrated. A vow in language forbidding it to himself as an offering, but he did not consecrate it as an offering (see Hilchot Nedarim 1:1-2).
therefore it has no redemption. Since it is forbidden only to him, it does not become consecrated by the vow but remains ordinary and cannot be redeemed from its prohibition for him.

this loaf is sacred or an offering etc.. With this wording he forbade the loaf to everyone, by consecrating it to the Temple treasury. Therefore anyone who eats of it commits me'ilah, and it can be redeemed from the consecration like all Temple-upkeep consecrations.
there was before him an ownerless loaf and he said, this loaf is consecrated. And when he said so, the Temple treasury acquired it.

he took it in order to eat it, he committed me'ilah by its full value. When he took it to eat it he transferred it from the Temple treasury's ownership to his own, and therefore he committed me'ilah with all of it.

in order to bequeath it, he committed me'ilah by the value of the benefit in it. When he took it in order that others acquire it, he had not yet removed it from the Temple treasury's ownership, and therefore did not commit me'ilah with all of it. However, he benefited from the consecrated property to the extent of the benefit he will receive from the one to whom he intends to transfer it (Ri Kapach).
one who receives this gift commits me'ilah when he uses it. When he uses the loaf.
for the giver is not forbidden it. The giver (the one who made the vow) does not commit me'ilah, since the loaf is not forbidden to him at all and he may transfer it to whomever he wishes.
and all things forbidden to him by such a vow combine. Just as altar offerings and Temple-upkeep consecrations combine with one another for me'ilah (below 5:2).
an offering until they are cut. Since he said so, even if he redeems them from the consecration, sanctity takes effect on them again.

and once they are cut they do not require redemption. For the consecration was only until they were cut, and when they were cut the consecration ended (for the sanctity of value is annulled without redemption - Bavli Nedarim 29a).
but if another redeemed them, they leave to ordinary status etc.. For one cannot stipulate and consecrate what is in the possession of others (Rosh, Nedarim 30a).
to strengthen the upkeep. To use it in the Temple.
one who consecrates to the altar something fit for Temple upkeep. And that is not fit for the altar.
there is me'ilah in all of them from the moment they are consecrated. Anything with monetary value is consecrated for Temple upkeep from the moment of its consecration and there is me'ilah in it.
